1.title: Exam Formats, Visual Practice and Final Strategy
1.text: Welcome to Module 14, the last module. You know the content. Now we turn that knowledge into exam technique. In Part 1, we cover the question formats and how to read cases, graphics and scenarios. In Part 2, we practice interactive items, and finish with your study plan and exam day.

1.title: What This Module Adds
1.text: Module 0 introduced the exam. This module adds technique. Part 1 teaches you to read questions, handle all eight formats, and read the graphics. Part 2 gives you five items in the interactive formats, and the final strategy. Knowledge gets you to the question. Technique gets you to the answer.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Know the eight question formats and how each is answered. Read a case and a graphic the efficient way. Spot the four distractor types in real options. Recall the best-answer patterns for fourteen situations. Practice five interactive-format items. And plan your last weeks and your exam day.

1.title: How the Exam Is Laid Out
1.text: Here is the layout. The exam opens with a case-study section, then the independent questions, with two ten-minute breaks. There are one hundred eighty questions in two hundred forty minutes, about eighty seconds each. Ten of the questions are unscored pretest items. Once you start a break, you cannot return to the earlier section. So flag and revisit items only inside the section you are in, and finish your review before each break.

1.title: Pacing Checkpoints
1.text: Use checkpoints. At eighty seconds a question, thirty questions take about forty minutes. Sixty take eighty. Ninety take a hundred twenty. And a hundred twenty take a hundred sixty. The full one hundred eighty questions use the two hundred forty minutes. Pace is an average. Spend less on easy items so that case and calculation items can get more. And if you are behind at a checkpoint, flag the hard items and move on, inside your section.

1.title: Eight Question Formats
1.text: The outline lists eight question types. Four are offered in every delivery mode: multiple choice with a single response, multiple response, case or scenario, and graphic-based. Four exist only in computer-based testing at a test center: matching, enhanced matching, point and click, and pull-down lists. Case and graphic items are new in twenty twenty-six. Be ready for all eight, because you may not know which ones you will get.

1.title: Multiple Choice and Multiple Response
1.text: Multiple choice with a single response asks for the one best answer. Use the patterns in this module. Multiple response asks for every correct answer. Judge each option on its own against the stem, and do not stop at the first correct one. Read how many answers are asked for. And remember that wrong options are rarely nonsense: they usually follow one of the distractor types.

1.title: Case or Scenario Questions
1.text: A case gives one situation, in text, tables or charts, followed by a series of questions. Read the questions first, so you know what to look for. Then read the case, and note the facts that matter: the approach, the roles, the constraints, the state and the dates. Then answer each question on its own. Some facts are noise, and each question usually depends on only a few of them.

1.title: Case Check-In: Reading a Case
1.text: Try it on our microgrid. A new tariff rule is announced while the dashboard team is mid-iteration. The facts that matter: it is a hybrid project, the rule takes effect in twelve months, and baseline changes go to the change board. The noise: a council member likes the canopy design, and a press visit is next month. Then ask: is the question about the first, next or best action? What state is it in? And who has the authority?

1.title: Graphic-Based Questions
1.text: For a graphic, take four steps. Read the title, the axes and the legend first. Name the quantity that is plotted. Calculate from the data shown, rather than judging by eye. Then ask what decision the graphic supports. The longest path, the likeliest threat, or the largest count is often not the answer. Read a Pareto chart by cost, not by count.

1.title: Matching and Enhanced Matching
1.text: Matching items pair two lists. Enhanced matching drags items onto locations in an image, or matches items to two lists at once. Start with the surest pairs, then use them to work out the rest. Some choices are decoys, and most choices are used once. Check whether a choice may be reused. And do not force a match: extra choices are there to be left unused. In enhanced matching, the second match often depends on the first.

1.title: Point and Click, and Pull-Down Lists
1.text: In point and click, you click the hotspot on an image that answers the question. Work out the value first: the highest score, the first month over a limit, or the lowest probability. Note what is being maximized or minimized. In a pull-down list, you choose from a drop-down in each row. The same options often repeat across rows, so decide each row on its own facts.

1.title: Habits for the Interactive Formats
1.text: Five habits for the interactive formats. Check the convention before you calculate: a network starting at day zero uses early finish equals early start plus duration, while PMBOK 8 counts from day one. Use the item's own start. Apply the rule printed in the item, such as authority limits or thresholds, not what you remember. Calculate, do not eyeball. In sequences, the formal step comes first. And do not force a match.

1.title: Reading a Scenario Question
1.text: Here is the method for any scenario. Find the approach: predictive, agile or hybrid. Find the ask: the first action, the next action, the best action, what should have been done, or which tool or term. Find the state: has it happened or might it, is there a baseline, and who has the authority? Remove the distractors, and keep the option that treats the cause and respects the process. And never choose by length or position.

1.title: Distractors in Action
1.text: See the four types in action. A misunderstanding of the vision keeps recurring in the steering group. Sending another detailed email treats the symptom. Reviewing the charter and the minutes analyzes instead of engaging. Asking the sponsor to instruct the group escalates too early. Meeting the people involved to ask what is unclear is the best answer. The fourth type, acting without analysis, would be rewriting the vision alone.

1.title: What the Best Answer Usually Does: Part 1
1.text: Seven patterns. A recurring misunderstanding or silence: meet or ask the people involved first, then analyze the cause. Two parties in disagreement: bring them together to agree, and decide directly only for safety or compliance. A change request or a free improvement: assess the impact, then use change control or the backlog, and never implement an unapproved change. On track, but the market changed: revalidate the value with the sponsor. A missing threshold: define it with the sponsor. A mandatory rule against a deadline: comply, and take exceptions through governance. An ethical dilemma: disclose, refuse, correct your errors, report facts, and protect confidentiality.

1.title: What the Best Answer Usually Does: Part 2
1.text: Seven more. A risk that has occurred: treat it as an issue, log it, run the planned response, and update the register. A team at a stage: direction for a new team, facilitation in storming, delegation for a mature team, without giving up accountability. Healthy metrics but poor outcomes: add outcome and leading measures. Knowledge about to leave: capture from people first, and transfer hands-on. An AI tool's output: a human validates it and stays accountable. Missing sustainability: raise it with the sponsor and write measurable indicators. Handover: get formal acceptance and confirm the receiver can run the result.

1.title: Words That Steer the Answer
1.text: Underline the words that steer the answer. First, next and best each ask something different. Assumption words choose a formula, such as the variance was a one-off. State words separate what has occurred from what might occur. Authority words, like threshold, sponsor and board, tell you who decides. Approach words, like baseline, backlog and iteration, tell you the mechanism. And hasty actions, such as deciding alone or acting now, often mark distractors.

1.title: Graphics to Practice Reading: Schedule, Cost and Flow
1.text: Now graphics to practice reading. First, schedule, cost and flow. A critical path network: the longest path, total and free float, and the effect of a delay. Burndown and burnup charts: remaining against completed work, and scope growth against slow progress. A Kanban board: work-in-progress limits and bottleneck columns. A cumulative flow diagram: a widening band is the bottleneck. Earned value curves: the gaps give the variances. The EAC formulas, by assumption. And a story map: the backbone, the release slices and any gap.

1.title: Graphics to Practice Reading: Risk, Quality, Value and Status
1.text: Next, risk, quality, value and status. A control chart: in or out of control, the rule of seven, and control against specification limits. A probability and impact matrix: scores and thresholds. A decision tree: branch values, including the cost of the choice. An NPV example: which project to choose, and why. The Kano model: satisfaction curves and the present or absent table. A status dashboard: red, amber and green, with explanations when a measure is outside its threshold. And a resource histogram: over-allocation, smoothing and leveling.

1.title: Graphics to Practice Reading: People, Structure and Knowledge
1.text: Last, people, structure and knowledge. Know these graphics well. The power and interest grid: manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor. The engagement assessment matrix: current against desired engagement, and the gap. The salience model: seven classes from power, legitimacy and urgency. RACI and hierarchy charts: one accountable owner, and the hundred percent rule. The Tuckman ladder: the team's stage and the matching style. Complexity zones: agreement against certainty. And the SECI model: the mode from the starting and ending form of the knowledge.

1.title: Part 1 Recap
1.text: Let us recap Part 1. There are eight formats, four of them only at a test center. For cases, read the questions first, then note the facts that matter. For graphics, read, name the quantity, calculate and decide. For interactive items, take the surest pairs first and apply the rule printed in the item. The method is approach, ask and state, then remove the distractors. And fourteen situations each have one usual best action. In Part 2, we practice five interactive items, then plan the final weeks.

2.title: Format Practice 1: Matching
2.text: Part 2 begins with practice. Format practice one: matching. This format appears at a test center. The five terms on the left are the burndown chart, the control chart, the power and interest grid, the probability and impact matrix, and the resource histogram. The six descriptions on the right are lettered A to F. Match each term to its description. One description is a decoy, so do not force a match. Pause the video and decide.

2.title: Matching: The Answers
2.text: Here are the answers. The burndown chart shows remaining work against time. The control chart shows whether a process is stable. The power and interest grid ranks stakeholders to set engagement effort. The probability and impact matrix ranks risks. And the resource histogram shows allocated hours against capacity. The description of steps and time to find waste belongs to a value stream map, so it was the decoy. Start with the surest pairs, and leave the decoy unmatched.

2.title: Format Practice 2: Pull-Down Lists
2.text: Format practice two: pull-down lists. For each situation, choose the best first action from the list. The four situations are these. A risk that the register listed is now late. A small dashboard change inside the committed scope of a hybrid project. Cost and schedule on track, but a new tariff rule changes the business case. And a free battery upgrade that is not in the approved design. The five actions are lettered A to E. The same option can appear in more than one row, and one option may not be needed at all. Decide each row on its own facts. Pause the video and decide.

2.title: Pull-Down: The Answers
2.text: The answers. Row one: a risk that the register listed has occurred, so it is an issue. Treat it as an issue and run the planned response. Row two: a small request inside the committed scope of a hybrid project goes to the product owner, who reprioritizes the backlog. Row three: cost and schedule are on track, but the business case changed, so revalidate the value with the sponsor. Row four: even a free upgrade is a change, so assess the impact and use change control. Escalation was the decoy.

2.title: Format Practice 3: Point and Click
2.text: Format practice three: point and click. Five threats, A to E, are plotted by probability across and impact up. Click the threat with the highest score, probability times impact. Work out the value first, then click. Pause the video and decide.

2.title: Point and Click: The Answer
2.text: The answer is threat B. Zero point three times zero point four is zero point one two. C scores zero point one zero, E zero point zero eight, A zero point zero seven, and D zero point zero four five. The likeliest threat is D, and the largest impact is E, but neither has the highest score. That is why you calculate first and click second.

2.title: Format Practice 4: A Graphic-Based Item
2.text: Format practice four: a graphic-based item. This burnup chart shows completed work rising by twenty points a sprint, while the scope line has climbed from one hundred twenty to one hundred seventy points. What does the chart show? The four options, A to D, are on the screen. Pause the video and decide.

2.title: Graphic-Based: The Answer
2.text: The answer is B. Scope has grown by fifty points, while the pace has stayed steady at twenty points a sprint. About two and a half sprints of work remain. A is wrong because the pace has not slowed. C is wrong because the original plan no longer holds. And D is wrong because completed work does not rise with scope. The next step is to talk with the product owner about priorities, and to take it to the sponsor if a threshold is crossed.

2.title: Format Practice 5: Sequence
2.text: Format practice five: a sequence, in the style of a drag-and-drop item. Put the change control steps in order. The seven cards, A to G, are on the screen. One card is a decoy. Remember that the formal step comes first. Pause the video and decide.

2.title: Sequence: The Answer
2.text: The order is: log the request. Assess the impact and recommend. Decide at the right level. Communicate the decision. Implement and update the documents. Then verify the result and close the request. Implementing while the request is pending is a shortcut that skips every step. Decoys in sequence items are almost always shortcuts.

2.title: Your Practice Plan
2.text: Your practice plan has four steps. Learn the foundations first, then each domain. Practice by topic: answer each scenario before reading the explanation, then note which pattern or distractor caught you. Simulate with timed mixed sets, then a mock exam. And in the last week, redo only the topics you miss. Throughout, review every miss for the pattern, not for the right letter.

2.title: Simulate and Review
2.text: Simulate the exam. Take timed mixed sets, for example sixty questions in about eighty minutes, following the domain weights. Then take a full mock exam under exam conditions. Review every miss for the pattern, not the answer. Redo the formulas with the quick reference cards. And practice the interactive formats as well as multiple choice. Remember that real items can be longer and may combine ideas, while practice items test one idea in a short setting.

2.title: The Last Week
2.text: In the last week, redo only the topics where you miss more than a third of the scenario questions. Re-read the best-answer patterns and the four distractor types. Use the quick reference cards the day before. Do not start new material. And rest before the exam. If any source disagrees with the content outline or PMBOK 8, follow the outline and PMBOK 8.

2.title: Exam Day
2.text: On exam day, pace yourself at about eighty seconds a question, and do not stay stuck. In the case section, read the questions first, then the case. Flag and review only inside your current section, and remember that a break closes the section behind you. For interactive items, apply the rule printed in the item. And before you book, confirm the current format, fees and eligibility on PMI's official site.

2.title: What You Have Covered
2.text: Look back at the whole course. Modules one to three gave you the foundations: projects, life cycles, tailoring, ethics, sustainability and AI. Modules four and five covered people: vision, stakeholders, communication and teams. Modules six to nine covered process: initiating, planning, executing, status and closure. Modules ten to twelve covered the business environment: governance, compliance, risk, issues, change and the external environment. And modules thirteen and fourteen gave you the numbers and the exam technique.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Let us recap the module. The formats: eight types, including the four that appear only at a test center. Reading: find the approach, the ask and the state, and in a case read the questions first. The distractors: treat the symptom, analyze instead of engaging, escalate too early, and act without analysis. The patterns: the usual best action in fourteen situations. And practice: simulate the exam, and review every miss for the pattern. Now it is time for the last test in this course. Five questions follow. For each one, pause the video, choose your answer, and then listen to the explanation.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. A matching item has five terms and six descriptions. You are sure of three pairs and unsure about the other two. What is the best approach? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. Start with the surest pairs and use them to work out the rest. Some choices are decoys, so a choice may stay unused. Not every description must be used. And a break closes the section, so you cannot return after it.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. You are about to start the case-study section, which has a long text and several questions. What is the best way to use your time? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. Reading the questions first tells you which facts to look for, and each question usually depends on only a few facts. Reading twice wastes time, skipping the case ignores its facts, and memorizing every number is unnecessary.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Two engineers have argued about the controller design for a week, and the sprint work has stalled. You have not yet spoken to either of them. What should you do first? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. The first move is to engage the people involved and help them agree. Deciding directly is for safety or compliance. Escalating too early, deciding alone and analyzing documents each avoid talking with the people involved.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Cost and schedule indices are on track, but the market assumed in the business case has closed. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. On time and on budget is not enough when the market or need changes, so the value is revalidated with the sponsor. Continuing ignores the lost value, replanning does not recover it, and cancelling is a decision for governance.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A team member wants to paste confidential meeting minutes into a public AI tool to summarize them. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. Use approved tools, keep confidential data out of public tools, and have a human validate the output and stay accountable. Allowing it exposes confidential data. A blanket ban ignores approved tools. Deleting the summary later does not undo the exposure.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: D. Sure pairs first. Leave decoys unused. Question two: B. Questions first, then the case, then the facts. Question three: A. Bring the parties together to agree. Question four: C. A changed market means revalidating the value. Question five: B. Approved tools only. A human validates the output. That completes Module 14. Good luck on exam day.
